FFMI Calculator

FFMI tells you how much lean mass you carry for your height, which makes it the BMI that actually works for lifters. Enter height, weight and body fat percentage.

What FFMI measures

The fat-free mass index takes your lean mass and divides it by your height squared, the same way BMI does with total weight. Because fat is removed first, FFMI reflects how much muscle (plus bone and water) you have built rather than how heavy you are.

That makes it far more useful than BMI for anyone who trains. A muscular 90 kg lifter at 12% body fat and an untrained 90 kg person at 30% share a BMI. Their FFMI scores are several points apart.

How to use the calculator

Enter your height, your current body weight and your body fat percentage. Body fat is the input that matters most, so use the best estimate you have: a DEXA scan, a skinfold measurement by someone experienced, or our body fat calculator, which uses the US Navy tape method.

The calculator returns your lean mass, your raw FFMI, your height-normalised FFMI and a category. Compare the normalised figure with the table below.

Advertisements

The formulas

Lean mass (kg) = weight (kg) × (1 − body fat % / 100)

FFMI = lean mass (kg) / height (m)²

Normalised FFMI = FFMI + 6.1 × (1.8 − height (m))

The normalisation step comes from the original research. Taller people naturally score a little lower on a height-squared index, so the adjustment scales everyone to a reference height of 1.80 m. If you are shorter than 1.80 m your normalised score drops slightly. If you are taller it rises.

Worked example: 80 kg at 15% body fat and 1.78 m tall gives 68 kg of lean mass. 68 / 1.78² = 21.5, and 21.5 + 6.1 × 0.02 = 21.6 normalised.

Reading your FFMI

These ranges apply to men. For women, subtract roughly 3 points from each boundary as an approximate guide, since women carry less lean mass on average at the same height.

Normalised FFMI (men)What it usually means
Below 18Below average muscle mass
18-20Average, typical of untrained men
20-22Above average, a few years of consistent training
22-23Excellent, clearly muscular
23-25Superior, advanced natural lifter
25-27Rare without performance-enhancing drugs
Above 27Very unlikely to be achieved naturally

Most men who start lifting sit somewhere around 18-20. Gaining two or three points over the first few years is a realistic target for someone who trains hard and eats well.

The natural limit debate

FFMI became famous because of a 1995 study by Kouri, Pope and colleagues, which compared male athletes who used anabolic steroids with those who did not. The non-users topped out around a normalised FFMI of 25, while many users exceeded it.

That number is often treated as a hard ceiling. It is not. It was a single sample of American gym-goers in the early 1990s, and a small number of genetically gifted athletes exceed 25 without drugs. What it does tell you is that a score in the mid-20s or higher is exceptional, and that comparing yourself to physiques far beyond it may mean comparing against a different set of rules.

If your score jumps by more than half a point in a month, check your body fat input first. A body fat estimate that is 3% too low adds roughly a point of FFMI on its own.

Realistic FFMI progress over time

Muscle gain is fastest at the start and slows every year after. That pattern shows up clearly in FFMI. A beginner can add a full point in a good first year, while an advanced lifter might take two or three years to add the same.

Training ageTypical FFMI gain per year (men)Notes
Year 11-2 pointsRapid early muscle gains
Year 20.5-1 pointStill steady with a good program
Years 3-40.3-0.6 pointsProgress needs planned overload
Year 5+0.1-0.3 pointsSmall, hard-won gains

These are approximations to set expectations, not promises. Starting point, age, sleep, diet and consistency all shift them. Women typically gain at a similar relative rate from a lower starting point.

Because the gains get small, measurement error starts to hide them. A one point change in body fat estimate can swamp a year of real progress for an advanced lifter. That is why it helps to track strength in a few main lifts, photos and tape measurements alongside FFMI. If all of them are moving the right way, the muscle is coming, whatever a single scan says.

If you are well below 20 and have been training for a while, the usual culprits are too little food, too little protein, or a program without enough hard sets. The guide to sets and reps for muscle growth and the protein calculator are good places to check first.

Limitations

FFMI inherits every error in your body fat number. Bioimpedance scales are particularly noisy, and a lean, muscular person is exactly who they tend to misread. Lean mass also includes water and glycogen, so creatine supplementation or a carb load can add a fraction of a point without any new muscle.

The categories describe population averages, not your potential. Frame size, limb length and age all play a role. Use FFMI to track your own trend over months rather than to rank yourself against strangers online.

What to do next

If you want to raise your FFMI, you need two things: a training plan built on progressive overload and enough food to grow. The push/pull/legs plan suits intermediate lifters, and the bulking vs cutting guide explains how to time a surplus. Set your daily numbers with the macro calculator.

Frequently asked questions

What is a good FFMI for a natural lifter?

For men, a normalised FFMI of 22-23 is a strong result that takes several years of serious training. Scores of 23-25 are advanced. For women, roughly 3 points lower is a fair comparison.

Is an FFMI of 25 really the natural limit?

It is a guideline from one 1995 study, not a law. Very few drug-free lifters exceed it, but some do, and measurement error in body fat can easily move a score by a point either way.

Why is my normalised FFMI different from my FFMI?

The normalised score adjusts for height so that tall and short people can be compared fairly. It adds 6.1 times the difference between 1.8 m and your height.

Can women use the FFMI calculator?

Yes. The formula is the same, but the categories in the table are based on men. Subtract around 3 points from each boundary for a rough female equivalent.

How often should I check my FFMI?

Every two to three months is enough. Lean mass changes slowly, and checking more often mainly picks up noise from your body fat measurement and water weight.

References

  1. Kouri EM, Pope HG Jr, Katz DL, Oliva P. Fat-free mass index in users and nonusers of anabolic-androgenic steroids. Clin J Sport Med. 1995.
  2. Schutz Y, Kyle UU, Pichard C. Fat-free mass index and fat mass index percentiles in Caucasians aged 18-98 y. Int J Obes. 2002.
